name: The Dismemberment Plan
label: DeSoto
lede: A D.C. band that recorded its best-known album on Interscope's money, got dropped in the merger, and watched it come out on a Jawbox alumni's label anyway.

eras.title: Named after a line in Groundhog Day
eras.text: Four guys from northern Virginia high schools start a band in 1993 and end up on DeSoto Records, the D.C. label run by two Jawbox alumni. The first drummer leaves after the debut, and the lineup that lasts arrives.

years.h: The band takes its name from an insurance plan in Groundhog Day
years.p: [[Travis Morrison|b9ba9319-c5c7-4316-b32a-d3f92a673e1f]], [[Eric Axelson|ecc42a4f-e214-40f1-af6d-6cdcade19702]], Jason Caddell and Steve Cummings start in D.C.; three of them went to Lake Braddock Secondary School in Burke, Virginia.
years.xp: The name comes from a 1993 Groundhog Day scene in which an insurance policy called the dismemberment plan gets a mention. Cummings, Morrison and Caddell had gone to school together in Burke, Virginia, and Axelson also attended Lake Braddock.

years.h: Can We Be Mature? EP, the first record
years.p: An EP that predates the first album by a year.

years.h: !, the debut, on DeSoto
years.p: The first album on DeSoto Records. Steve Cummings leaves afterward; Joe Easley takes over on drums.
years.xp: Joe Easley takes over the drums in 1995 and stays for the rest of the band's run. From here the band is Morrison, Caddell, Axelson and Easley.

eras.title: Terrified, then signed to a major
eras.text: A second record, then a two-album deal with Interscope. A big label budget and three weeks in a New Jersey studio produce the record that made the band's name. Nobody at the label would be there to release it.

years.h: The Dismemberment Plan Is Terrified on DeSoto
years.p: The second album, a jumpier and funnier record than the debut, and the one that got the major labels calling.

years.h: Interscope signs the band to a two-album deal
years.p: The money is real major-label money. So is the merger that follows.
years.xp: Seagram bought PolyGram in May 1998. Universal then folded Geffen and A&M into Interscope, which is how a two-album deal for a D.C. indie band ended up inside a company that was restructuring around it.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Dismemberment Plan · PopMatters: Emergency & I at 25
yt: The Ice of Boston, live on KEXP (2013)
years.h: The Ice of Boston EP, Interscope's only release
years.p: The one record Interscope officially puts out, and Wikipedia's account says it repackages a track.
years.xp: According to the band's Wikipedia entry, the EP was the only item Interscope released during the deal. PopMatters describes it as pointing toward Emergency & I with humor, isolation and a big chorus.

eras.title: Dropped, then a best-of-the-year
eras.text: The label that paid for the record vanishes before it can release it. DeSoto puts it out anyway, and it turns into the record the band gets remembered for.

years.big: Everyone they worked with got fired.
q: I'm glad we got dropped, it's not sour grapes.
years.src: Wikipedia: Emergency & I · Chip Midnight: The Dismemberment Plan (2000)
years.h: Interscope drops the band, and pays them $50,000
years.p: They learn in April 1999, on tour with [[Burning Airlines|5ea472eb-5040-410c-b021-1e678276aed9]], that they are among the acts cut after the Universal merger.
years.xp:
Wikipedia reports the band received $50,000 owed on the second album of the deal. Axelson told Chip Midnight that everyone they had dealt with at the label was gone by then.

The band came out of it with a finished record, no debt and DeSoto ready to release it.

years.h: The City, live, February 6, 1999
years.p: Captured months before the album is out and before Interscope drops the band.

years.h: Emergency & I, released by DeSoto
years.p: Recorded on Interscope's budget, released by a label run out of D.C. by two ex-Jawbox members.
years.xp:
Main tracking was three weeks at Water Music in Hoboken, New Jersey, with more work at Inner Ear Studios in Arlington, Virginia; [[J. Robbins|3babd931-a940-43a8-b629-d7aed5b821d9]] and [[Chad Clark|f3f09e99-e31c-4aa2-99e4-0b4e59e72f87]] produced, per Wikipedia. Morrison made the cover art on a computer at Water Music between sessions.

Pitchfork's Brent DiCrescenzo gave it 9.6 out of 10 and told readers to buy it right away. In 2011 the site raised the score to 10 for the Barsuk vinyl reissue.

years.src: Washington City Paper: [Your Band] Played Here
years.h: Two men in nine-foot costumes at Fort Reno
years.p: A Pikachu and a box labeled Box of Pubes, both from Baltimore, show up at the band's 1999 free show in Fort Reno Park.
years.xp: David Arbury tells the Washington City Paper's Fort Reno oral history that two guys came in nine-foot costumes, one in a tall box with a hole for his face, inspired by a recent Conan O'Brien sketch.

eras.title: Pearl Jam, and a slower record
eras.text: The next two years take the band across Europe as an opener and into a darker, slower album. It's also where cracks show.

years.h: Pearl Jam invite the band to open in Europe
years.p: Morrison finds the email from Pearl Jam's management, calls the number, and reaches an Indian restaurant.
years.xp: After the right number turned up, the offer was three weeks in Europe starting June 14 in Prague. Axelson told Chip Midnight that some of the festival dates were in fields holding tens of thousands of people, with the band on early in the day.

years.src: Wikipedia: Change · Vice: Looking Back on Change
years.h: Change, made at Inner Ear with J. Robbins
years.p: Slower, darker and more gothic, Morrison says, than the record before it. Pitchfork names it 14th album of 2001.
years.xp: Robbins engineered and Clark mixed. Morrison has said he can hear the Pearl Jam tour in the heavier songs, naming Time Bomb and Secret Curse, and that he heard the wheels coming off the band halfway through writing.

eras.title: Ending it at the top
eras.text: With new songs that don't excite them, the band calls it and plays a farewell that is heavy on fan requests.

years.src: Washington City Paper: What Do You Want Them to Say? · Wikipedia: The Dismemberment Plan
years.h: The band announces its breakup
years.p: January 19, 2003: the new songs weren't working, so they stop, with a farewell run to come.
years.xp: Caddell told the Washington City Paper the reason was creative: they did not know how to make a record without music that excited them, and what they were writing was not doing that.

years.src: Washington City Paper: [Your Band] Played Here · Wikipedia: The Dismemberment Plan
years.h: The last Fort Reno show is stopped by lightning
years.p: Axelson remembers getting through about eight songs before rain and gear trouble ended it.
years.xp: Axelson tells the Washington City Paper's oral history: they got off maybe eight songs, gear got wrecked, and there was lightning, which was not a safe thing to be doing. Wikipedia lists the July 28 show as cancelled; the oral history has them playing a partial set.

years.src: Perfect Sound Forever: Travis Morrison · Wikipedia: The Dismemberment Plan
years.h: Last show: a sold-out 9:30 Club, nearly all requests
years.p: Two hours, most of it chosen by the crowd.
years.xp: Perfect Sound Forever describes the farewell as an unheard-of two hours of nearly all requests.

eras.title: Solo years and a benefit
eras.text: Morrison releases a solo album that gets a zero from Pitchfork, Axelson starts Maritime, and one weekend at the Black Cat sells out fast.

years.h: Travistan gets a 0.0 from Pitchfork
years.p: Morrison's first solo record is scored 0.0 by the site that had given Emergency & I a 9.6.
years.xp: Perfect Sound Forever reports independent record stores stopped stocking it, and describes the score as one the site was said to have avoided repeating. Morrison later fronted a band called the Hellfighters and moved to New York.

years.h: Eric Axelson forms Maritime with ex-members of the Promise Ring
years.p: Glass Floor is the first Maritime album, in 2004; two more follow in 2006 and 2007.

years.src: Washingtonian: Travis Morrison on Reuniting · Washington City Paper: What Do You Want Them to Say?
years.h: One-off reunion at the Black Cat, for Callum Robbins
years.p: A benefit for the son of J. Robbins. It sells out in four minutes.
years.xp: Morrison told Washingtonian that the band had said at the breakup they would consider benefit shows if they still enjoyed the songs. He also said they were far more popular after breaking up than before.

eras.title: The reunion that stuck
eras.text: A reissue turns into a tour, and the tour turns into a new album.

years.src: Wikipedia: Emergency & I · Wikipedia: The Dismemberment Plan
years.h: The Washington Post reports the band will reunite
years.p: Axelson says there are no plans for a new record, only shows.
years.xp: The shows were tied to the Barsuk vinyl reissue of Emergency & I, which followed on January 11, 2011 with four bonus tracks and oral-history liner notes.

years.h: Late Night with Jimmy Fallon
years.p: The band plays The City on network TV during the reissue run.

years.h: Pitchfork Festival and the Roots Picnic
years.p: Ten more dates beyond the three D.C. shows in January, including Chicago and Philadelphia.

years.h: Uncanney Valley, the first album in twelve years
years.p: On Partisan. The single Waiting arrives with a phone number for fans to call.
years.xp: The number promoted was 252-64-DPLAN. Singles Waiting, Invisible and Daddy Was a Real Good Dancer came out between July and September.

eras.title: Twenty-five years of Emergency & I
eras.text: A cover for a Dischord tribute leads to six anniversary shows.

years.h: The band covers Circus Lupus on a Dischord tribute
years.p: Unrequited, recorded in August 2023, closes the loop with the D.C. scene that raised them.

years.h: Six shows for twenty-five years of Emergency & I
years.p: Dates include Best Friends Forever in Las Vegas and United Sounds in New York.
